stimulus: Manager: Our cafe's loyalty-card program is working. In the six months since we introduced the cards, the average number of monthly visits per cardholder has been well above the average number of monthly visits per customer in the six months before the program began. Clearly, the cards are encouraging people to come in more often.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the manager's argument?
choice_a: Loyalty-card programs have failed to increase overall sales at most cafes that have tried them.
choice_b: Several cardholders say that the promise of rewards is what first led them to visit the cafe more frequently.
choice_c: A nearby cafe that introduced a loyalty program at the same time has seen an even larger increase in visits per cardholder.
choice_d: The customers who signed up for loyalty cards were, even before the program began, visiting the cafe far more often than the average customer.
choice_e: The cafe's loyalty cards are printed on recycled stock that costs slightly more than standard card material.
prediction_text: The comparison is cardholders now versus all customers before. Attack that link: cardholders may simply be the frequent visitors.
trap_a: attacks a broader claim about sales at other cafes (survivor)
trap_c: comparison to another cafe leaves the link intact
trap_e: cost detail with no bearing on the reasoning
explanation_a: Other cafes' sales results concern a different claim; this argument is about visit frequency at this cafe.
explanation_b: Testimony that rewards drove extra visits supports the manager's conclusion rather than weakening it.
explanation_c: Another cafe's larger gain does not disturb the inference drawn from this cafe's numbers.
explanation_d: Correct. If sign-ups were already the most frequent visitors, the cardholder average would exceed the old overall average even if the cards changed nothing - the comparison collapses.
explanation_e: Printing costs are irrelevant to whether the cards increase visits.
